As of 2014, New York City had an estimated population of 8,491,079, marking a record high. Since the 2010 United States Census, the city has experienced a net increase in residents, with more people moving in than leaving. Between April 2010 and July 2014, New York City added 316,000 inhabitants, the largest growth among all U.S. cities during that period. The city’s population is more than double that of the next largest city in the country, despite New York City occupying a smaller geographic area. Approximately 40% of New York State’s residents live in New York City, and the city’s population also represents a similar proportion of the total population in the New York metropolitan region.

In the 1970s, job losses due to industrial restructuring caused New York City to suffer from economic problems and rising crime rates. By the mid 1990s, crime rates started to drop dramatically due to revised police strategies, improving economic opportunities, gentrification, and new residents, both American transplants and new immigrants from Asia and Latin America. Important new sectors, such as Silicon Alley, emerged in the city's economy. New York's population reached all-time highs in the 2000 Census and then again in the 2010 Census.

Beginning with the fifth-generation iPod, Apple added a feature that lets users set a maximum volume, addressing worries about potential hearing damage. In European Union countries, the sixth-generation iPod restricts the top volume output to 100 decibels. Previously, Apple was required to recall iPods from a market where the volume exceeded the legally permitted threshold. Reports from late 2013 indicate that buyers of new sixth-generation iPods discovered a new setting enabling them to turn off the EU volume restriction. This capability was made possible by updated software included with these newer devices. In contrast, earlier sixth-generation iPods cannot install this software update and therefore remain subject to the original volume limitation.

Commercial solar water heaters began appearing in the United States in the 1890s. These systems saw increasing use until the 1920s but were gradually replaced by cheaper and more reliable heating fuels. As with photovoltaics, solar water heating attracted renewed attention as a result of the oil crises in the 1970s but interest subsided in the 1980s due to falling petroleum prices. Development in the solar water heating sector progressed steadily throughout the 1990s and has continued to grow since 1999. Although generally underestimated, solar water heating and cooling is by far the most widely deployed solar technology with an estimated capacity of 154 GW as of 2007.

Beginning in 1236, the Mongol prince Kublai, who later ruled as Khagan from 1260–1294, was granted a large territory in North China by his superior. Karma Pakshi, 2nd Karmapa Lama (1203–1283)—the head of the Karma Kagyu lineage of Tibetan Buddhism—declined Kublai's invitation, so Kublai instead invited Drogön Chögyal Phagpa (1235–1280), who was related to Sakya Pandita, to his court in 1253. Kublai established a special relationship with the Phagpa lama, recognizing Kublai as the leading authority in political matters and the Phagpa lama as his chief religious advisor. Kublai also appointed Drogön Chögyal Phagpa as the director of a government agency overseeing Buddhist and Tibetan affairs and as the priest-king of Tibet, which included thirteen states ruled by myriarchies.

Chopin's public popularity as a virtuoso began to wane, as did the number of his pupils, and this, together with the political strife and instability of the time, caused him to struggle financially. At his last Paris concert, he performed with the cellist Auguste Franchomme, and together they played three movements of the Cello Sonata Op. 65.

The city receives 49.9 inches of precipitation annually, which is fairly spread throughout the year. Average winter snowfall between 1981 and 2010 has been 25.8 inches (66 cm), but this varies considerably from year to year. Hurricanes and tropical storms are rare in the New York area, but are not unheard of and always have the potential to strike the area. Hurricane Sandy brought a destructive storm surge to New York City on the evening of October 29, 2012, flooding numerous streets, tunnels, and subway lines in Lower Manhattan and other areas of the city and cutting off electricity in many parts of the city and its suburbs. The storm and its profound impacts have prompted the discussion of constructing seawalls and other coastal barriers around the shorelines of the city and the metropolitan area to minimize the risk of destructive consequences from another such event in the future.

New York is a major center for political fundraising in the United States, with four out of the five ZIP codes contributing the most to political campaigns located in Manhattan. One particular ZIP code accounted for the highest amount of donations to both major presidential candidates during the 2004 election. There is a notable imbalance in the financial relationship between the city and both state and federal governments. For every dollar New York City pays in federal taxes, it receives only 83 cents in services, resulting in the city sending billions more to the federal government each year than it gets back. Additionally, New York City contributes $11 billion more annually to the state government than it receives in return.

There are seven state parks within the confines of New York City, including Clay Pit Ponds State Park Preserve, a natural area which includes extensive riding trails, and Riverbank State Park, a 28-acre (110,000 m2) facility that rises 69 feet (21 m) over the Hudson River.

The Fire Department of New York (FDNY) is responsible for fire suppression, technical rescue operations, initial response to biological, chemical, and radiological incidents, as well as emergency medical care throughout all five boroughs of New York City. As the largest municipal fire department in the United States, FDNY ranks second globally in size. The department has a workforce of around 11,080 uniformed firefighters and more than 3,300 uniformed emergency medical technicians and paramedics. The official motto associated with the department is "New York's Bravest."

Reaction to the novel varied widely upon publication. Despite its popularity and frequent use in education, there has been relatively little literary analysis of it. One author compiled personal reflections on To Kill a Mockingbird from various writers and public figures, describing the book as "an astonishing phenomenon." In 2006, British librarians ranked the novel as one "every adult should read before they die," placing it at the top of their list. The book was adapted into an Oscar-winning film in 1962, with direction and screenplay handled by notable figures in the film industry. Since 1990, a play based on the novel has been performed annually in the town where the author grew up.

In the fourth fiscal quarter of 2008, Apple disclosed that iPod sales contributed just 14.21% to the company’s total revenue. During a keynote event in September 2009, it was revealed that more than 220 million iPods had been sold cumulatively by that time. The steady drop in iPod purchases, which began in 2009, was anticipated by Apple’s Chief Financial Officer at the time, Peter Oppenheimer, who stated in June 2009: “We expect our traditional MP3 players to decline over time as we cannibalize ourselves with the iPod Touch and the iPhone.” From 2009 onward, iPod sales consistently fell each financial quarter, and notably, 2013 marked the first year since the iPod’s launch that no new model was released.

New York City is the most-populous city in the United States, incorporating more immigration into the city than outmigration since the 2010 United States Census. More than twice as many people live in New York City as in the second-most populous U.S. city, and within a smaller area. New York City's population amounts to about 40% of New York State's population and a similar percentage of the New York metropolitan area population.

At the upper boundary of the atmosphere, Earth is exposed to 174,000 terawatts (TW) of solar energy. Roughly 30% of this incoming radiation is reflected back into space by the atmosphere. The sunlight that reaches the Earth's surface is primarily distributed within the visible and near-infrared wavelengths, with a smaller fraction in the near-ultraviolet range. In most inhabited regions, daily solar energy received typically ranges from 150 to 300 watts per square meter, which is equivalent to about 3.5 to 7.0 kilowatt-hours per square meter per day.
The New York Islanders and the New York Rangers are two hockey teams based in New York City. The New Jersey Devils are another team in the region, playing in Newark.

The Battle of Long Island, the largest battle of the American Revolutionary War, was fought in August 1776. After the Americans were defeated in this battle, a series of smaller armed engagements followed. The city then became the British military and political base of operations in North America. It served as a haven for Loyalist refugees and for escaped slaves who joined the British lines, seeking the freedom promised by the Crown to all fighters. During the British occupation, as many as 10,000 escaped slaves crowded into the city. When British forces evacuated at the close of the war in 1783, they transported 3,000 freedmen for resettlement in Nova Scotia, and others were resettled in England and the Caribbean.

New York City is home to the Brooklyn Nets, an NBA franchise. The city’s women’s basketball team is known as the New York Liberty. The National Invitation Tournament, the earliest national collegiate basketball championship, was first hosted in New York in 1938 and continues to be held there. Basketball is deeply ingrained in the city’s culture, with games taking place in almost every park and many local youths advancing to prominent college teams and the NBA.

As of 2013, two major global advertising agencies based in Manhattan had combined annual revenues of approximately US$21 billion, reflecting New York City's role as the top global center for the advertising industry, which is metonymously referred to as "Madison Avenue." The city's fashion industry provides approximately 180,000 employees with $11 billion in annual wages.

New York City is the most-populous city in the United States, with an estimated record high of 8,491,079 residents as of 2014, incorporating more immigration into the city than outmigration since the 2010 United States Census. More than twice as many people live in New York City as in the second-most populous U.S. city (Los Angeles), and within a smaller area. New York City gained more residents between April 2010 and July 2014 (316,000) than any other U.S. city. New York City's population amounts to about 40% of New York State's population and a similar percentage of the New York metropolitan area population.

Beyoncé's fan base is known as the Bey Hive, a name inspired by the word "beehive" and intentionally spelled to resemble her first name. Before adopting this title, her fans were referred to by a different name. The term Bey Hive emerged after discussions and petitions on social media platforms and coverage in online news during various competitions.

Frédéric François Chopin (French pronunciation: [fʁe.de.ʁik fʁɑ̃.swa ʃɔ.pɛ̃]; /ˈʃoʊpæn/; born Fryderyk Franciszek Chopin) was born on either 22 February or 1 March 1810 and died on 17 October 1849. He held both Polish and French nationalities—Polish by birth and French through his father’s citizenship. Chopin was a celebrated composer and virtuoso pianist of the Romantic period, recognized worldwide for his exceptional artistry and technical mastery, which set him apart from his contemporaries. His compositions were chiefly written for solo piano. Chopin was born in the Duchy of Warsaw and spent his formative years in Warsaw, which became part of Congress Poland after 1815. Displaying remarkable musical talent from a young age, he completed his musical studies and produced his earliest compositions in Warsaw. At the age of 20, just weeks before the November 1830 Uprising began, he left Poland.

In August 2006, Apple and Creative reached a settlement to resolve their legal disputes. As part of the agreement, Apple agreed to pay Creative a substantial sum for a license related to Creative's patent. The arrangement also allowed Apple to recover some of its payment under certain conditions. Following the settlement, Creative announced plans to produce iPod accessories by joining a program designed for third-party manufacturers.

In 1785, New York was designated the national capital after the end of the war. It served as the final capital under the Articles of Confederation and became the first capital city when the United States Constitution was adopted. In 1789, George Washington, the nation’s first President, was sworn into office; during the same year, both the inaugural session of the United States Congress and the first meeting of the Supreme Court took place, and the Bill of Rights was composed—all within the city. By 1790, New York City had become the most populous city in the country.

Between 907 and 960, China experienced the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, a time marked by political fragmentation. During this era, Tibet was also experiencing significant internal turmoil, resulting in minimal interaction between the two regions; consequently, there are few records of Sino-Tibetan relations from this time. In the subsequent Song dynasty, which lasted from 960 to 1279, documentation of contact between China and Tibet remains scarce. The Song dynasty’s primary focus was on defending against northern adversaries, specifically the Liao dynasty, which was ruled by the Khitan people from 907 to 1125, and the Jin dynasty, governed by the Jurchens from 1115 to 1234.

In December, Beyoncé joined various celebrities to produce a video campaign for "Demand A Plan," a bipartisan initiative by hundreds of US mayors and others, aiming to influence federal gun control laws after the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting. Beyoncé became an ambassador for the 2012 World Humanitarian Day campaign, donating her song "I Was Here" and its music video, filmed at the UN, to support the cause. In 2013, it was announced that Beyoncé would collaborate with Salma Hayek and Frida Giannini on Gucci's "Chime for Change" campaign, which promotes female empowerment. A concert for the cause was held on June 1, 2013, in London, with performances by artists such as Ellie Goulding, Florence and the Machine, and Rita Ora. In 2013, Omnicom Group and Interpublic Group, two of the world’s largest advertising agencies based in Manhattan, together generated about US$21 billion in annual revenue. This highlights New York City’s prominence in the global advertising sector. The fashion industry in New York City employs around 180,000 people and pays out roughly $11 billion in wages each year.

Twilight Princess takes place several centuries after Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask, and begins with a youth named Link who is working as a ranch hand. One day, the village is attacked by Bulblins, who carry off the village's children with Link in pursuit before he encounters a mysterious barrier of Twilight. A Shadow Beast pulls him beyond the barrier into the Realm of Twilight, where he is transformed into a wolf and imprisoned. Link is soon freed by an imp-like Twilight being named Midna, who dislikes Link but agrees to help him if he obeys her unconditionally. She guides him to Princess Zelda. Zelda explains that Zant, the King of the Twilight, has stolen the light from several Light Spirits and conquered Hyrule. In order to save Hyrule, Link must first restore the Light Spirits by entering the Twilight-covered areas and, as a wolf, recover what was lost. As he restores them, the Light Spirits return Link to his Hylian form.

During the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period of China (907–960), there was little interaction between China and Tibet. Few records of contacts between the two regions exist from the Song dynasty (960–1279). The Song focused their attention on northern enemy states, such as the Liao dynasty (907–1125) and the Jin dynasty (1115–1234), which were ruled by the Khitan and the Jurchen, respectively.

Despite his success as a producer, West's true aspiration was to be a rapper. Though he had developed his rapping long before he began producing, it was often a challenge for West to be accepted as a rapper, and he struggled to attain a record deal. Multiple record companies ignored him because he did not fit the dominant image in mainstream hip hop at the time. After a series of meetings with a major label, West was ultimately denied an artist deal.

Major tourist destinations include Times Square; Broadway theater productions; the Empire State Building; the Statue of Liberty; Ellis Island; the United Nations Headquarters; museums such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art; greenspaces such as Central Park and Washington Square Park; Rockefeller Center; Chinatown in Manhattan; luxury shopping along notable avenues; and events such as the Halloween Parade in Greenwich Village; the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade; the lighting of the Rockefeller Center Christmas Tree; the St. Patrick's Day parade; seasonal activities such as ice skating in Central Park in the wintertime; the Tribeca Film Festival; and free performances in Central Park at Summerstage. Major attractions in the boroughs outside Manhattan include Flushing Meadows-Corona Park and the Unisphere in Queens; the Bronx Zoo; Coney Island in Brooklyn; and the New York Botanical Garden in the Bronx. A large ferris wheel was under construction at the northern shore of Staten Island in 2015, offering views of the harbor and city skyline.

New York City is located in southeastern New York State. The city lies at the mouth of the Hudson River, which has contributed to its development as a major trading port. Most of New York City is built on three islands: Long Island, Manhattan, and Staten Island. The city is adjacent to the Atlantic Ocean.

Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts is located in Lincoln Square on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. The Lee Strasberg Theatre and Film Institute is situated in Union Square, and Tisch School of the Arts is part of New York University. Central Park SummerStage offers free performances of plays and music in Central Park.

The Battle of Long Island, a major engagement of the American Revolutionary War, took place entirely within the modern-day borough of Brooklyn. After the Americans were defeated in this battle, a series of smaller armed engagements followed. The city subsequently became the British military and political base of operations in North America. It served as a haven for Loyalist refugees, as well as escaped slaves who joined the British lines in pursuit of freedom promised by the Crown to those who fought for them. When the British forces evacuated at the close of the war in 1783, they transported many freedmen for resettlement in Nova Scotia, England, and the Caribbean.

In 1785, the assembly of the Congress of the Confederation made New York the national capital shortly after the war. New York was the last capital of the U.S. under the Articles of Confederation and the first capital under the Constitution of the United States. In 1789, the first President of the United States, George Washington, was inaugurated; the first United States Congress and the Supreme Court of the United States each assembled for the first time, and the United States Bill of Rights was drafted, all at Federal Hall on Wall Street. By 1790, New York had become the largest city in the United States.

New York, often called New York City to distinguish it from the State of New York, is the most populous city in the United States. It forms the heart of the New York metropolitan area and is recognized as one of the world’s most densely populated urban centers. As a major global hub, New York exerts significant influence in commerce, finance, media, art, fashion, research, technology, education, and entertainment. The city’s famously fast pace has inspired the phrase “New York minute.” New York is also home to the headquarters of the United Nations, making it an important site for international diplomacy. Frequently described as both the cultural and financial capital of the world, New York holds a prominent position on the global stage.

The National Park Service oversees both the Statue of Liberty National Monument and the Ellis Island Immigration Museum, which are located in the states of New York and New Jersey. These sites share the harbor with Governors Island National Monument, situated in New York. On Manhattan Island, several historic locations are federally administered, including Castle Clinton National Monument, Federal Hall National Memorial, Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site, General Grant National Memorial—commonly known as "Grant's Tomb"—African Burial Ground National Monument, and Hamilton Grange National Memorial. In addition, numerous privately owned sites are recognized on the National Register of Historic Places or as National Historic Landmarks, such as the Stonewall Inn in Greenwich Village, which is widely regarded as the birthplace of the modern LGBT rights movement.

The terms also specified that Apple could recover a portion of this payment if Creative succeeded in licensing the patent to other companies. Following the settlement, Creative revealed plans to manufacture iPod accessories by participating in the Made for iPod program, which allows third-party vendors to sell iPod-compatible products.

Historically, the city is known for the New York Cosmos, the highly successful former professional soccer team which was the American home of Pelé, one of the world's most famous soccer players. A new version of the New York Cosmos was formed in 2010 and began play in 2013. The Cosmos play their home games at James M. Shuart Stadium on the campus of Hofstra University.

A draft of To Kill a Mockingbird, known as Go Set a Watchman, was controversially released to the public in mid-2015. This manuscript, completed several years before the publication of Mockingbird, is set decades after the events depicted in To Kill a Mockingbird but does not continue the original narrative. The story centers on an adult Scout Finch who returns from New York to visit her father, Atticus Finch, in Maycomb, Alabama, where she faces the intolerance present in her hometown. The Watchman manuscript was thought to be lost until it was discovered by Harper Lee's lawyer, Tonja Carter, though this account has been the subject of debate. Watchman features early versions of many characters familiar from To Kill a Mockingbird. Lee's agent, Andrew Nurnberg, once stated that Mockingbird was intended as the first in a trilogy, with Watchman as the final installment and a shorter novel to connect them. However, this claim has been challenged by rare books expert James S. Jaffe, who examined the manuscript and concluded it was simply another draft of To Kill a Mockingbird. Jonathan Mahler also described Watchman as merely the initial draft of Mockingbird, noting that many passages are nearly identical between the two works.

Starting in mid-2007, United, Continental, Delta, and Emirates became the first four major airlines to sign agreements to equip their aircraft with iPod seat connections. This complimentary service enables travelers to charge and power their iPods, as well as access their music and video collections directly through the personal seat-back screens. Initially, KLM and Air France were mentioned as potential partners in Apple’s initiative, but both airlines subsequently clarified that they were only considering the addition of these features and had not committed to the 2007 agreement.

The Hudson River runs through the Hudson Valley and empties into New York Bay. From New York City up to Troy, New York, it functions as an estuary. This river forms the boundary between New York City and the state of New Jersey. The East River, a tidal strait, connects Long Island Sound to the Upper New York Bay and divides the Bronx and Manhattan from Long Island. Separating most of Manhattan from the Bronx is the Harlem River, another tidal strait that links the Hudson and East Rivers. The Bronx River, which passes through both the Bronx and Westchester County, is the city’s only purely freshwater river.

Beginning in 1236, the Mongol prince Kublai—who would later become Khagan and rule from 1260 to 1294—received a substantial appanage in northern China from his overlord, Ögedei Khan. Karma Pakshi (1203–1283), who was the second Karmapa Lama and the leader of the Karma Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism, declined Kublai’s invitation. As a result, Kublai turned to Drogön Chögyal Phagpa (1235–1280), the nephew and successor of Sakya Pandita, inviting him to his court in 1253. Kublai established a distinctive partnership with Phagpa, whereby Kublai was acknowledged as the supreme authority in political matters, while Phagpa served as his chief religious advisor. Furthermore, Kublai appointed Drogön Chögyal Phagpa as the head of the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs and as the priest-king of Tibet, which at that time consisted of thirteen states governed by myriarchies.

The largest engagement of the American Revolutionary War, known as the Battle of Long Island, took place entirely within what is now Brooklyn. Following the American defeat in this battle, several smaller skirmishes ensued, and New York City became the central military and political headquarters for the British in North America. During the British occupation, the city served as a refuge for Loyalists and also attracted escaped slaves, who were drawn by the British promise of freedom to those who fought for their cause. When the Revolutionary War concluded and the British army began to withdraw and evacuate the city, they relocated some freed individuals to Nova Scotia, while others were resettled in England and the Caribbean.

The former county seat of Beichuan was left uninhabited and is now maintained as part of the Beichuan Earthquake Museum. In Dujiangyan, eight schools collapsed. The novel To Kill a Mockingbird was first published in 1960. It quickly achieved critical acclaim, earning the Pulitzer Prize and establishing itself as a cornerstone of contemporary American literature. The author drew inspiration for the story’s plot and characters from personal experiences, particularly from people in their family and neighborhood, and from a real-life incident that took place close to their hometown in 1936, when they were ten.

With the death of Zhengde and the rise of his successor, the politics at court shifted in favor of the Neo-Confucian establishment, which not only rejected the Portuguese embassy of Fernão Pires de Andrade, but also harbored animosity towards Tibetan Buddhism and lamas. Evelyn S. Rawski, a professor in the Department of History at the University of Pittsburgh, writes that the Ming's unique relationship with Tibetan prelates essentially ended during this period, while Ming influence in certain regions was supplanted by other powers.

Although Tom is found guilty, Bob Ewell feels disgraced by the outcome of the trial, with Atticus noting that he had "destroyed [Ewell's] last shred of credibility at that trial." Seeking revenge, Ewell spits in Atticus' face, attempts to break into the judge's residence, and harasses Tom Robinson's widow. Ultimately, Ewell ambushes Jem and Scout as they walk home at night following the school’s Halloween pageant. During the attack, Jem’s arm is broken, but in the midst of the chaos, someone intervenes to save the children. The mysterious rescuer carries Jem back to the Finch home, where Scout realizes the identity of their savior.

During the years immediately following the novel's publication, Harper Lee enjoyed the attention its popularity brought her, granting interviews, visiting schools, and attending events honoring the book. In 1961, when To Kill a Mockingbird was in its 41st week on the bestseller list, it received significant literary recognition, which surprised Lee. That same year, it was also honored by the National Conference of Christians and Jews, and in 1962, it was named Paperback of the Year by Bestsellers magazine. Starting in 1964, Lee began to turn down interviews, expressing that the questions had become monotonous, and grew uneasy with the level of attention she was receiving. From that point on, she declined to speak with reporters about the book. She also consistently refused to provide an introduction, writing in 1995: "Introductions inhibit pleasure, they kill the joy of anticipation, they frustrate curiosity. The only good thing about Introductions is that in some cases they delay the dose to come. Mockingbird still says what it has to say; it has managed to survive the years without preamble."

Many significant American cultural movements originated in New York City, including the Harlem Renaissance, which was instrumental in shaping the African-American literary canon in the United States. During the 1940s, New York was a hub for jazz music, while the 1950s saw the rise of abstract expressionism as a leading artistic style in the city. The 1970s marked the emergence of hip hop, a new musical genre that began in New York. Additionally, the city’s punk and hardcore music scenes gained prominence throughout the 1970s and 1980s. New York has also maintained a vibrant tradition of Jewish American literature.

During the 1970s, New York City faced major economic challenges and a surge in crime as a result of widespread job losses caused by changes in the industrial sector. Although the financial industry experienced a revival in the 1980s that significantly boosted the city's economy, crime rates continued to climb throughout that decade and into the early 1990s. It was not until the mid-1990s that crime began to decline sharply, a change attributed to updated policing methods, better economic prospects, gentrification, and an influx of new residents, including both domestic migrants and immigrants from Asia and Latin America. The 1990s also saw the rise of new economic sectors in New York, such as Silicon Alley. The city’s population reached record levels in the 2000 Census and set another new peak in the 2010 Census.

Uniquely among major American cities, New York is divided between, and is host to the main branches of, two different US district courts: the District Court for the Southern District of New York, whose main courthouse is on Foley Square near City Hall in Manhattan, and the District Court for the Eastern District of New York, whose main courthouse is in Brooklyn. The US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit and US Court of International Trade are also based in New York, also on Foley Square in Manhattan.

At the end of the Second Anglo-Dutch War, the English gained New Amsterdam (New York) in North America in exchange for Dutch control of Run, an Indonesian island. Several intertribal wars among the Native Americans and some epidemics brought on by contact with the Europeans caused sizable population losses for the Lenape between the years 1660 and 1670. By 1700, the Lenape population had diminished to 200.

According to the Köppen climate classification system, New York City is characterized by a humid subtropical climate (Cfa) when applying the 0 °C (32 °F) isotherm for its coldest month, which is January. This makes it the northernmost major city in North America to be classified as such. The suburbs located just north and west of the city are situated in a transitional area between the humid subtropical (Cfa) and humid continental (Dfa) climate zones. On average, New York enjoys sunshine on 234 days each year, receiving about 57% of the possible sunlight annually, which totals approximately 2,535 hours of sunshine per year. The city is designated as USDA Plant Hardiness Zone 7b.

iPods have been criticized for their allegedly short life-span and fragile hard drives. A 2005 survey conducted on the MacInTouch website found that the iPod line had an average failure rate of 13.7%, though they noted that comments from respondents suggested the actual failure rate might be lower. The survey concluded that some models were more durable than others. In particular, iPods with hard drives tended to have failure rates above 20%, while those using flash memory had rates below 10%. In late 2005, many users complained that the surface of the first generation iPod Nano could become scratched easily, making the screen unusable. A class action lawsuit was also filed. Apple initially considered the issue a minor defect.[citation needed]

Commercial solar water heaters saw increasing use in the United States until the 1920s, but were gradually replaced by cheaper and more reliable heating fuels. As with photovoltaics, solar water heating attracted renewed attention as a result of the oil crises in the 1970s, but interest subsided in the 1980s due to falling petroleum prices. Development in the solar water heating sector progressed steadily throughout the 1990s, and growth rates have averaged 20% per year since 1999. Although generally underestimated, solar water heating and cooling is by far the most widely deployed solar technology, with an estimated capacity of 154 GW as of 2007.

This group rejected a foreign embassy and maintained a longstanding hostility toward Tibetan Buddhism and its lamas. According to historian Evelyn S. Rawski, the Ming dynasty’s unique relationship with Tibetan prelates effectively ended during Jiajing’s reign, as outside influence replaced Ming authority in certain regions.

Situated on a major natural harbor, New York City consists of five boroughs, each functioning as its own county within New York State. These boroughs—Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island—make up the city as a unified municipality. Census estimates from the mid-2010s indicate that New York City had a population of over 8 million people living within an area of just 305 square miles (790 km²), making it the most densely populated major city in the United States. Residents of New York speak up to 800 different languages, making it the most linguistically diverse city in the world. The metropolitan area surrounding New York City remains the largest in the country, with a Combined Statistical Area population of over 23 million. In terms of economic output, the region’s gross metropolitan product ranks first in the nation and is comparable to the economies of some of the world’s largest countries.

The city's total area is 468.9 square miles (1,214 km²). Of this, 164.1 square miles (425 km²) is water. The highest point in the city reaches 409.8 feet (124.9 m) above sea level, with its summit mostly covered in woodlands as part of a large greenbelt.

Major attractions in the boroughs outside Manhattan include Flushing Meadows-Corona Park and the Unisphere in Queens; the Bronx Zoo; Coney Island; and the New York Botanical Garden in the Bronx. A large ferris wheel was under construction at the northern shore of Staten Island in 2015, overlooking notable city landmarks.

A brief shoot at London's City Hall took place in April 2015, while Mendes was on location. In May 2015, filming occurred on the water in London. Stunt scenes involving Craig and Seydoux on a speedboat, as well as a low-flying helicopter near Westminster Bridge, were shot at night, with filming temporarily closing both Westminster and Lambeth Bridges. Scenes were also shot near MI6's headquarters at Vauxhall Cross. The crew returned less than a week later to film scenes set solely on Westminster Bridge. A local organization was present on set to simulate rain and monitor smoke used for filming. Craig, Seydoux, and Waltz, as well as Harris and Fiennes, were seen being filmed. Prior to this, scenes involving Fiennes were shot at a restaurant in Covent Garden. Filming then took place in Trafalgar Square. In early June, the crew, along with Craig, Seydoux, and Waltz, returned to the water for a final time to continue filming scenes previously shot there.

Commercial solar water heaters saw increasing use in the United States until the 1920s, but were gradually replaced by cheaper and more reliable heating fuels. As with photovoltaics, solar water heating attracted renewed attention as a result of the oil crises in the 1970s, but interest subsided in the 1980s due to falling petroleum prices. Development in the solar water heating sector progressed steadily throughout the 1990s, and growth rates have averaged 20% per year since 1999. Although generally underestimated, solar water heating and cooling is by far the most widely deployed solar technology, with an estimated capacity of 154 GW as of 2007.

New York—often referred to as New York City or the City of New York to distinguish it from the State of New York, of which it is a part—is the most populous city in the United States and the center of the New York metropolitan area, ranking among the largest urban agglomerations in the world. A global power city, New York exerts a significant impact upon commerce, finance, media, art, fashion, research, technology, education, and entertainment, its fast pace defining the term New York minute. Home to the headquarters of the United Nations, New York is an important center for international diplomacy and has been described as the cultural and financial capital of the world.

Spectre was released on 26 October 2015 in the United Kingdom, followed by a worldwide release. It was released in the United States on 6 November 2015. It became the second James Bond film to be screened in IMAX venues after Skyfall, although it was not filmed with IMAX cameras. Spectre received mixed reviews upon its release; although criticised for its length, lack of screen time for new characters, and writing, it received praise for its action sequences and cinematography. The theme song, "Writing's on the Wall", received mixed reviews, particularly compared to the previous theme; it also received major music awards recognition. As of 20 February 2016, Spectre has grossed over $879 million worldwide.

Starting with the fifth-generation iPod, Apple introduced a feature allowing users to set a maximum volume, aiming to address concerns about hearing damage. In certain regions, including those within the European Union, the sixth-generation iPod included restrictions on how loud the device could play audio. Previously, Apple was required to recall iPods from the French market because their volume exceeded the legally permitted threshold. Reports from late 2013 noted that buyers of new sixth-generation iPods found a new setting that allowed them to disable the regional volume restriction. This option was available due to updated software on these newer devices. Earlier sixth-generation iPods, however, could not install this update and continued to be subject to the original volume limitation.

New York City's food culture features a wide range of international cuisines shaped by its diverse population. The city is known for foods such as bagels, cheesecake, and pizza, and offers a vast selection of restaurants, including Asian eateries, sandwich shops, diners, and coffeehouses. There are about 4,000 licensed mobile food vendors, many of which are immigrant-owned, serving popular street foods like falafel and kebabs. According to Michelin, New York is home to nearly one thousand of the finest and most diverse haute cuisine restaurants in the world. The New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene assigns letter grades to the city's 24,000 restaurants based on inspection results.

The Battle of Long Island, the largest battle of the American Revolutionary War, was fought in August 1776 entirely within the modern-day borough of Brooklyn. After the Americans were defeated in this battle, several smaller armed engagements followed. The city subsequently became the British military and political base of operations in North America. During the British occupation, the city served as a haven for Loyalist refugees and for escaped slaves who joined the British lines in pursuit of freedom promised by the Crown. When the war ended in 1783, the British evacuated their forces and resettled some freedmen in places such as Nova Scotia, England, and the Caribbean.

Despite Tom's conviction, Bob Ewell is humiliated by the events of the trial, Atticus explaining that he "destroyed [Ewell's] last shred of credibility at that trial." Ewell vows revenge, spitting in Atticus' face, trying to break into the judge's house, and menacing Tom Robinson's widow. Finally, he attacks the defenseless Jem and Scout while they walk home on a dark night after the school Halloween pageant. One of Jem's arms is broken in the struggle, but amid the confusion someone comes to the children's rescue. The mysterious man carries Jem home, where Scout realizes that he is Boo Radley.

Go Set a Watchman, an earlier version of To Kill a Mockingbird, was released to the public amid controversy on July 14, 2015. This manuscript, which was finished in 1957, takes place two decades after the events of To Kill a Mockingbird, though it does not serve as a direct sequel. The narrative centers on an adult Jean Louise “Scout” Finch, who returns from New York to visit her father, Atticus Finch, in Maycomb, Alabama, where she confronts the prejudice present in her hometown. The manuscript for Watchman was thought to be lost until it was reportedly found by Harper Lee’s attorney, Tonja Carter, a claim that has been the subject of much debate. Watchman features early incarnations of several characters later seen in To Kill a Mockingbird. Lee’s agent, Andrew Nurnberg, stated that Mockingbird was initially meant to be the first in a trilogy, with Watchman as the final installment and a shorter novel to connect them; however, this idea has been challenged by rare books specialist James S. Jaffe. After examining the manuscript for Lee’s lawyer, Jaffe determined that Watchman is simply another draft of To Kill a Mockingbird. Similarly, Jonathan Mahler described Watchman as merely the initial draft of Mockingbird, and the significant overlap between the texts, sometimes even identical passages, further undermines the trilogy claim.

Each year, the Earth’s atmosphere, oceans, and land absorb around 3,850,000 exajoules (EJ) of solar energy. Of this vast amount, roughly 3,000 EJ annually is harnessed by photosynthesis and stored in biomass. The yearly amount of solar energy that reaches Earth’s surface is so great that it equals about twice the total energy that could ever be extracted from all of the planet’s non-renewable resources combined.

Following the discovery of a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Wii version of Twilight Princess, an exploit was developed that allowed the execution of custom code from a Secure Digital (SD) card on the console. A specially crafted save file would cause the game to load unsigned code, which could include Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) programs and homebrew Wii applications. Versions 3.3 and 3.4 of the Wii Menu prevented copying exploited save files onto the console until circumvention methods were discovered, and version 4.0 of the Wii Menu patched the vulnerability.

The novel To Kill a Mockingbird was first published in 1960. The book quickly achieved critical acclaim, earning the Pulitzer Prize and establishing itself as a cornerstone of contemporary American literature. The author drew inspiration for the story’s plot and characters from personal experiences, particularly from people in their family and neighborhood, and from a real-life incident that took place close to their hometown in 1936, when they were ten.

During the 1970s, New York City faced major economic challenges and a surge in crime as a result of widespread job losses caused by changes in the industrial sector. Although the financial industry experienced a revival in the 1980s that significantly boosted the city's economy, crime rates continued to climb throughout that decade and into the early 1990s. It was not until the mid-1990s that crime began to decline sharply, a change attributed to updated policing methods, better economic prospects, gentrification, and an influx of new residents, including both domestic migrants and immigrants from Asia and Latin America. The 1990s also saw the rise of new economic sectors in New York, such as Silicon Alley. The city’s population reached a record level in the 2000 Census.

From a young age, West showed a strong interest in the arts, beginning to write poetry at just five years old. His mother remembered noticing his enthusiasm for drawing and music when he was in third grade. As he grew up in the city, West became heavily involved in the local hip hop community. He started rapping while in third grade and began creating his own music by seventh grade, eventually selling his compositions to other musicians. At thirteen, West wrote a rap song titled "Green Eggs and Ham" and convinced his mother to pay $25 per hour for studio time in a modest basement studio, where the microphone was suspended from the ceiling with a wire hanger. Although this was not her preference, his mother still supported his ambitions. Early in his career, West met a producer and DJ who soon became his mentor, teaching him how to sample and program beats after West received his first sampler at the age of fifteen.

As of 2013, the global advertising agencies of Omnicom Group and Interpublic Group, both based in Manhattan, had combined annual revenues of approximately US$21 billion, reflecting New York City's role as the top global center for the advertising industry, which is metonymously referred to as "Madison Avenue". The city's fashion industry provides approximately 180,000 employees with $11 billion in annual wages.

In 2004, Kanye West made headlines when he abruptly left the American Music Awards after failing to win the Best New Artist honor. However, his first major public controversy occurred shortly after the release of Late Registration, during a televised fundraiser for Hurricane Katrina survivors. In September 2005, West appeared as a presenter alongside actor Mike Myers at a nationally broadcast benefit event. While Myers stuck to the scripted remarks, West departed from the planned speech and, when given the opportunity to speak again, made a statement criticizing President George Bush. This moment was broadcast across the country, sparking widespread debate and prompting President Bush to later describe it as one of the most "disgusting moments" of his time in office. The following year, in January 2006, West generated additional controversy by appearing on the cover of Rolling Stone magazine, wearing a crown of thorns.

In December, Beyoncé, along with a variety of other celebrities, participated in a video campaign for "Demand A Plan," a bipartisan effort by a group of 950 US mayors and others designed to influence the federal government into rethinking its gun control laws, following the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting. Beyoncé became an ambassador for the 2012 World Humanitarian Day campaign, donating her song "I Was Here" and its music video, shot in the UN, to the campaign. In 2013, it was announced that Beyoncé would work with Salma Hayek and Frida Giannini on a Gucci "Chime for Change" campaign. The campaign, which aired on February 28, was set to her new music. A concert for the cause took place on June 1, 2013, in London and included other acts like Ellie Goulding, Florence and the Machine, and Rita Ora. In advance of the concert, she appeared in a campaign video released on May 15, 2013, where she, along with Cameron Diaz, John Legend, and Kylie Minogue, described inspiration from their mothers, while a number of other artists celebrated personal inspiration from other women, leading to a call for submission of photos of women of viewers' inspiration from which a selection was shown at the concert. Beyoncé said about her mother Tina Knowles that her gift was "finding the best qualities in every human being." Beyoncé is also taking part in "Miss a Meal," a food-donation campaign, and supporting Goodwill charity through online charity auctions at Charitybuzz that support job creation throughout Europe and the U.S.

To Kill a Mockingbird was Lee's only published book until Go Set a Watchman, an earlier draft of To Kill a Mockingbird, was published in 2015. Lee continued to respond to her work's impact until her death in February 2016.

Between 907 and 960, China experienced the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, a time marked by political fragmentation. In the following Song dynasty, which lasted from 960 to 1279, the main focus was on defending against northern adversaries, particularly the Liao dynasty and the Jin dynasty. The Liao dynasty was ruled by the Khitan people, while the Jin dynasty was governed by the Jurchens.

Italian designer Roberto Cavalli has noted that Beyoncé incorporates a variety of fashion styles to complement her music during performances. Her mother collaborated on a book released in 2002 called Destiny's Style, which details the influence of fashion on the group's achievements. The B'Day Anthology Video Album includes numerous scenes focused on fashion, highlighting both traditional and modern clothing choices. In 2007, Beyoncé appeared on the cover of a major swimsuit magazine, making her the second African American woman to do so, following Tyra Banks. Additionally, she has been recognized for her sense of style by various publications.

The FDNY headquarters is located at 9 MetroTech Center in Downtown Brooklyn, and the FDNY Fire Academy is located on Randalls Island. There are three Bureau of Fire Communications alarm offices which receive and dispatch alarms to appropriate units. One office, at 11 Metrotech Center in Brooklyn, houses Manhattan/Citywide, Brooklyn, and Staten Island Fire Communications. The Bronx and Queens offices are in separate buildings.

The plot and characters are loosely based on the author's observations of family and neighbors, as well as on an event that occurred near the author's hometown in 1936, during childhood.

Beginning in 1236, the Mongol prince Kublai, who later ruled as Khagan from 1260–1294, was granted a large territory in North China by his superior. Karma Pakshi, 2nd Karmapa Lama (1203–1283)—the head of the Karma Kagyu lineage of Tibetan Buddhism—declined Kublai's invitation, so Kublai instead invited Drogön Chögyal Phagpa (1235–1280), who was related to Sakya Pandita, to his court in 1253. Kublai established a special relationship with the Phagpa lama, recognizing Kublai as the leading authority in political matters and the Phagpa lama as his chief religious advisor. Kublai also appointed Drogön Chögyal Phagpa as the director of a government agency overseeing Buddhist and Tibetan affairs and as the priest-king of Tibet, which included thirteen states ruled by myriarchies.

Apple introduced a new version of the iPod Touch in 2015, officially launching it on the Apple Store in July of that year. This latest iPod Touch features several significant upgrades, including the advanced A8 processor and an improved display. Its processing core delivers performance more than five times faster than earlier models, making it comparable to the iPhone 5S. The newest iPod Touch is offered in five color options: space grey, pink, gold, silver, and Product (red).

New York City is the most-populous city in the United States, with an estimated record high of 8,491,079 residents as of 2014, incorporating more immigration into the city than outmigration since the 2010 United States Census. More than twice as many people live in New York City as in the second-most populous U.S. city (Los Angeles), and within a smaller area. New York City's population makes up a significant portion of both the New York metropolitan area and the state as a whole.

I Love New York (stylized I ❤ NY) is both a logo and a song that are the basis of an advertising campaign used to promote tourism in New York City, and later to promote New York State as well. The trademarked logo, owned by New York State Empire State Development, appears in souvenir shops and brochures throughout the city and state, some licensed, many not. The song is the state song of New York.

Several independent stereo brands, including JVC, Pioneer, Kenwood, Alpine, Sony, and Harman Kardon, have created ways for their systems to work with iPods. Other connection options involve using adapter kits or transmitters. It is important to note that some integration products are not permitted in certain countries. New York is a major center for political fundraising in the United States, with four out of the five ZIP codes contributing the most to political campaigns located in Manhattan. One particular ZIP code on the Upper East Side accounted for the highest amount of donations to both major candidates during the 2004 presidential election. There is a notable imbalance in the financial relationship between the city and both state and federal governments. For every dollar New York City pays in federal taxes, it receives only 83 cents in services, resulting in the city sending $11.4 billion more to the federal government each year than it gets back. Additionally, New York City contributes $11 billion more annually to the state government than it receives in return.

A play based on the novel has been performed annually in the author's hometown.

The Hudson River flows through the Hudson Valley into New York Bay. Between New York City and Troy, New York, the river is an estuary. The Hudson River separates the city from the U.S. state of New Jersey. The East River—a tidal strait—flows from Long Island Sound and separates parts of the city from Long Island. Another tidal strait, the Harlem River, connects the East and Hudson Rivers. The Bronx River, which flows through the Bronx and Westchester County, is the only entirely fresh water river in the city.

The Occupy Wall Street protests began on September 17, 2011, in Zuccotti Park, located in the Financial District of Manhattan. The demonstrations drew widespread attention and inspired a broader movement focused on social and economic issues.

Combined with the era’s political unrest and instability, these factors led to his financial difficulties. In February 1848, he performed his final concert in Paris alongside cellist Auguste Franchomme, during which they played three movements from the Cello Sonata Op. 65.

iPods have faced criticism regarding their supposedly limited lifespan and the vulnerability of their hard drives. In 2005, the MacInTouch website carried out a survey to determine how frequently iPods failed. Their findings showed an average failure rate of 13.7% across the iPod range, though they acknowledged that feedback from participants suggested the actual failure rate might be somewhat lower. The survey also revealed that certain models were sturdier than others; specifically, iPods equipped with hard drives had failure rates typically exceeding 20%, whereas those using flash memory experienced failure rates under 10%. Towards the end of 2005, a significant number of first generation iPod Nano owners reported that the device’s surface was prone to scratching, which could make the screen unreadable. This led to a class action lawsuit. Although Apple initially downplayed the issue as a minor flaw, the company eventually began including protective sleeves with these iPods to address the problem.

Truman Capote, a childhood friend of Harper Lee and a renowned author, contributed a statement for the first edition’s dust jacket, praising the novel as the work of “someone rare” with an exceptional sense of humor and a vivid outlook on life. Some have interpreted Capote’s remarks as implying that he either authored or significantly edited the book. In 2003, a newspaper in Tuscaloosa reported that Capote’s father claimed his son had written “almost all” of the novel. However, in 2006, a letter from Capote—donated to a literary heritage museum—revealed that in 1959 he told a neighbor that Lee was in the process of writing a book soon to be published. Additionally, extensive correspondence between Lee and her editor provides strong evidence against the speculation that Capote was the true author. Harper Lee’s older sister also addressed these rumors, dismissing them as “the biggest lie ever told.”

Starting with the fifth-generation iPod, Apple added a user-configurable volume limit in response to concerns about hearing loss. In the sixth-generation iPod, users noted that the maximum volume output level was restricted to 100 dB in EU markets. Previously, iPods were removed from sale in a country within the EU for exceeding this legal limit. Later, some users who purchased new sixth-generation iPods in late 2013 reported a new option that allowed them to disable the EU volume limit, which was made possible by updated software included with these devices. Older sixth-generation iPods could not update to this software version.

Beginning in mid-2007, four major airlines, United, Continental, Delta, and Emirates, reached agreements to install iPod seat connections. The free service will allow passengers to power and charge an iPod, and view video and music libraries on individual seat-back displays. Originally KLM and Air France were reported to be part of the deal with Apple, but they later released statements explaining that they were only contemplating the possibility of incorporating such systems.

The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess (Japanese: ゼルダの伝説 トワイライトプリンセス, Hepburn: Zeruda no Densetsu: Towairaito Purinsesu?) is an action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube and Wii home video game consoles. It is the thirteenth installment in the The Legend of Zelda series. Originally planned for release on the GameCube in November 2005, Twilight Princess was delayed by Nintendo to allow its developers to refine the game, add more content, and port it to the Wii. The Wii version was released alongside the console in North America in November 2006, and in Japan, Europe, and Australia the following month. The GameCube version was released worldwide in December 2006.[b]

The United States Open Tennis Championships, recognized as one of the four Grand Slam tournaments worldwide, takes place annually at the National Tennis Center in New York City. The New York Marathon ranks among the largest marathons globally, with the 2004, 2005, and 2006 races holding the records for the highest numbers of finishers; in 2006 alone, 37,866 runners completed the event. The Millrose Games, an annual track and field competition, is known for featuring the Wanamaker Mile as its signature race. Boxing maintains a strong presence in New York City’s sports culture, highlighted by the annual Amateur Boxing Golden Gloves tournament, which is held at a major arena in the city. The city is closely associated with a historic horse race, the final event of the Triple Crown series, which takes place at a racetrack just outside the city limits, typically on the first or second Sunday in June. Additionally, New York City has hosted major golf tournaments, including the U.S. Open and PGA Championships at notable nearby golf clubs.

New York City experiences an annual precipitation total of 1,270 millimeters (49.9 inches), with rainfall distributed relatively evenly throughout the year. The average snowfall during winter months, calculated from 1981 to 2010, is 66 centimeters (25.8 inches), though this amount can fluctuate significantly from one year to the next. While hurricanes and tropical storms seldom affect the New York region, they do occasionally occur and always pose a threat. On October 29, 2012, Hurricane Sandy struck New York City, unleashing a powerful storm surge that inundated streets, tunnels, and subway lines in Lower Manhattan and other neighborhoods, and caused widespread power outages across the city and its surrounding areas. The devastation caused by Sandy has led to ongoing discussions about building seawalls and other protective coastal structures along the city’s shoreline and throughout the metropolitan region to reduce the risk of similar disasters in the future.

In the fourth fiscal quarter of 2008, Apple disclosed that iPod sales contributed just 14.21% to the company’s total revenue. During a keynote event in September 2009, it was revealed that more than 220 million iPods had been sold cumulatively by that point. The steady drop in iPod purchases, which began in 2009, was anticipated by Apple’s Chief Financial Officer at the time, Peter Oppenheimer, who stated in mid-2009: “We expect our traditional MP3 players to decline over time as we cannibalize ourselves with the iPod Touch and the iPhone.” From 2009 onward, iPod sales consistently fell each financial quarter, and notably, 2013 marked the first year since the iPod’s launch that no new model was released.

Between 907 and 960, China experienced the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, a time marked by political fragmentation.
